content: Diabetes during pregnancy can lead to adverse outcomes for both the mother and the newborn. Exercise has been suggested as an additional approach to help improve blood sugar control in these cases. However, the impact of exercise on pregnancies complicated by diabetes requires thorough evaluation. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of exercise programs, either as a standalone intervention or combined with other treatments, compared to no specific exercise program or other therapies, on maternal and perinatal health outcomes. Additionally, the review aimed to determine whether exercise programs could reduce the need for insulin prescriptions to manage blood sugar levels. It also sought to compare the effectiveness of different types of exercise programs on maternal and perinatal health outcomes. To gather evidence, the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register was searched up to December 31, 2005. This search was later updated on October 1, 2009, with the new results added to a section awaiting classification. The review included all randomized controlled trials that evaluated the effects of exercise on perinatal outcomes and maternal health in pregnant women with diabetes. Relevant studies were assessed for inclusion and methodological quality. Data were extracted by three review authors, and analyses were conducted based on the principle of intention to treat. For dichotomous data, relative risks and 95% confidence intervals were calculated. The review included four trials involving a total of 114 pregnant women diagnosed with gestational diabetes. None of the trials included women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Participants were recruited during their third trimester, and the exercise interventions lasted approximately six weeks. These programs typically involved exercising three times per week for 20 to 45 minutes per session. The analysis found no significant differences in outcomes between the exercise programs and other treatment regimens. The authors concluded that there is currently insufficient evidence to either recommend or discourage the participation of pregnant women with diabetes in exercise programs. Further research is needed, particularly larger trials that include women with gestational diabetes as well as those with type 1 and type 2 diabetes, to better evaluate the potential benefits of exercise during pregnancy. It is also noted that the six studies awaiting classification may influence the conclusions of this review once they are assessed.
